task.description:
WF-03 Step 3 SECURITY GATE for ISS-0440. Apply your INV-1..INV-8 scope test and checks in full. This description names the run-specific risk.

WHAT CHANGED: lib/mix/tasks/letflow.lint_handoffs.ex gains a --dir <path> flag and a restricted --autofix mode; docs/agents/shared/HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md 1.3 gains a procedural clause. No application code, no tenant data path, no migration, no API route, no secrets (expected: INV-1..INV-8 largely NOT-APPLICABLE -- but confirm rather than assume, and say so explicitly).

THE REAL RISK HERE IS NOT TENANT DATA -- IT IS PIPELINE INTEGRITY, so assess it under that heading even though it is unusual for your role:

  1. --autofix REWRITES FILES IN PLACE. It mutates the pipeline's own audit record -- the handoff corpus that documents what every agent did and concluded. Assess: can it rewrite anything it should not? Verify the mapping is genuinely closed ({PASS, COMPLETE, DONE} -> COMPLETED only), that it touches ONLY the top-level status field and no other field, and that every rewrite is reported by path and old->new value rather than silent.
  2. THE FAIL REFUSAL IS THE SAFETY-CRITICAL PROPERTY. Silently converting a genuinely FAILED handoff to COMPLETED would falsify the pipeline's record of a failure -- worse than the violation being fixed. ORCH independently tested this and confirms: planting top-level status FAIL produced an [H1] violation, an 'AUTOFIX -- REFUSED (REQUIRES HUMAN-EQUIVALENT DECISION)' report naming the ambiguity, a non-zero exit, and a BYTE-IDENTICAL file (sha256 unchanged before/after). RE-DERIVE this yourself rather than accepting ORCH's test -- it is the one property whose failure would be worse than the original defect. Also probe the adjacent cases ORCH did not: a missing status key, a null status, a non-string status (number/list/object), and a status that is already legal but wrong for the file's actual state. Confirm none of them is silently rewritten.
  3. --autofix + --dir POINTED AT THE REAL CORPUS is an unreviewed mass-rewrite surface. The design deliberately does NOT restrict this, arguing that a restriction would reintroduce the 'agent must remember the safe flag' failure mode the whole issue exists to eliminate, and citing the closed map, status-field-only scope and per-file reporting as what bounds the risk. CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR judged that reasoning sound. Give your own SECURITY verdict on it -- a different question from the design-ergonomics one it was judged on. Consider specifically: could an agent or human run `--autofix` against the whole corpus and mass-rewrite history in a way that passes review unnoticed? Is the per-file reporting sufficient to make such a run visible in a diff?
  4. CI PATH INTEGRITY. This file is a HARD CI GATE every in-flight run on every host depends on -- there are concurrent Letflow sessions live on this workstation right now. Confirm the no-flag path is unchanged. ORCH verified `git diff main...HEAD -- mix.exs .github/workflows/ci.yml` is EMPTY (neither file touched) and that a no-flag run still reports 'OK -- 0 new violations ... (25 pre-existing grandfathered)'. Re-derive both.
  5. The implementer also threaded `dir` into check_registry_coverage/2, which was hardcoded to @handoffs_dir -- reportedly a no-op on the default path, done so H5 does not compute nonsense run_ids against a --dir fixture. This was NOT in the design. Verify it is genuinely a no-op by default and does not weaken H5's real-corpus behaviour.

Also confirm no new dependency, no network call, no shell-out, and no file write outside the explicit --autofix path.

You may READ anything. Do not edit lib/ or test/ except transiently for a probe you revert and verify (quote `git status --porcelain lib/ test/` empty if you do). Do NOT run --autofix against the real handoffs/ corpus -- use a scratch directory outside the repo, and say which. Complete the handoff with a clear PASS/FAIL and per-item verdicts; commit to branch feature/WF03-ISS0440-20260903.

result.summary:
Scope test: OUT OF SCOPE for INV-1..INV-9 -- git diff main...HEAD --name-only shows only lib/mix/tasks/letflow.lint_handoffs.ex, docs/agents/shared/HANDOFF_PROTOCOL.md, docs/issues/ISS-0441.yaml, this run's own handoffs/, and the design doc. No priv/repo/migrations/*.exs, no lib/letflow/ application code, no Ecto schema, no API route/controller/plug, no response-shaping code, no lookup-by-ID handler, no secret-resolving code (grepped for System.get_env/password/secret/token: zero hits in the changed file), no outbound HTTP client code (grepped httpc/HTTPoison/Finch/Req/hackney: zero hits), no raw SQL (grepped Repo./Ecto.: zero hits -- the only System.cmd calls in the file are pre-existing git-history queries for the H6 floor-commit mechanism, confirmed not present in this diff via `git diff ... | grep System.cmd` returning empty). Per-invariant verdicts: INV-1 NOT-APPLICABLE (no tenant-scoped table/schema/migration touched). INV-2 NOT-APPLICABLE (no API response type, S4 not started). INV-3 NOT-APPLICABLE (no scripting/plugin sandbox, S5 not started). INV-4 NOT-APPLICABLE (no secret resolution code; confirmed by grep, zero hits). INV-5 NOT-APPLICABLE (no lookup-by-ID endpoint, S4 not started). INV-6 NOT-APPLICABLE in its literal sense (no new tenant-data-access path) -- but its underlying SPIRIT (a mechanism proving its own claimed behaviour before merge) is exactly what I re-derived below rather than trusting either ORCH's or ELIXIR-DEV's self-report. INV-7 NOT-APPLICABLE (no SQL, confirmed by grep). INV-8 NOT-APPLICABLE (no external-I/O bare match pattern introduced; the pre-existing System.cmd git calls already handle non-zero/error results via case matching, unmodified by this diff). INV-9 NOT-APPLICABLE (no outbound HTTP, confirmed by grep).

Assessed instead under PIPELINE INTEGRITY, per the handoff's framing, with five run-specific items, all independently re-derived (I did not accept ORCH's or ELIXIR-DEV's tests as given):

1. AUTOFIX SCOPE -- CONFIRMED CLOSED. Read autofix_file/1 (lines 414-446) and write_json!/2 (454-457) directly. The map is exactly {PASS,COMPLETE,DONE}->COMPLETED, FAIL is hardcoded to a separate refuse clause (not in the map), and write_json!/2 does `data |> Map.put("status", to)` -- Map.put on a key that already exists replaces only that key, provably touching no other field. Verified empirically on a probe fixture (see item 2): sha256 of the resulting file's decoded content shows every field except top-level `status` byte-for-byte identical, and result.status (the nested, free-text field) was NOT touched -- it stayed "PASS" while top-level status flipped to "COMPLETED", exactly the two-field distinction the whole issue exists to enforce. Every rewrite is reported by path and old->new value via print_autofix_report/1 (line 459) -- confirmed in my own run's output, not assumed.

2. FAIL REFUSAL -- RE-DERIVED INDEPENDENTLY, CONFIRMED, PLUS FIVE ADJACENT CASES ALSO CONFIRMED SAFE. Built my own probe fixtures from scratch (not reusing ORCH's), in a scratch directory OUTSIDE the repo (C:/Users/tvolo/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/.../scratchpad/iss440-probe, well outside c:/Users/tvolo/dev/ai-dala/letflow-2 -- never committed, deleted after use, confirmed via git status --porcelain showing zero stray entries). Hashed every fixture (sha256sum) before running `mix letflow.lint_handoffs --dir <probe> --autofix`, then re-hashed after. Results: FAIL -> byte-identical hash, exit 1, output under a distinct 'AUTOFIX -- REFUSED (REQUIRES HUMAN-EQUIVALENT DECISION)' heading naming the file, the literal value "FAIL", and the ambiguity reason verbatim. Missing status key -> byte-identical hash, refused, reason 'missing or non-string top-level status (nil)'. Explicit null status -> byte-identical hash, refused, same reason (Jason decodes JSON null to Elixir nil, so this is the same code path as missing -- confirmed by reading Map.get/2's behavior: both a missing key and an explicit null value return nil). Non-string status: number (42) -> byte-identical hash, refused, reason names the literal '42'. List (['PASS','FAIL']) -> byte-identical hash, refused, reason names the literal list. Object ({'weird':'shape'}) -> byte-identical hash, refused, reason names the literal map. Bonus case: an unrecognized-but-plausible string ('PLACEHOLDER_STATUS', legal-string-shaped but not in @legal_statuses and not in the autofix map) -> byte-identical hash, refused. Legal-but-semantically-wrong case (top-level 'PENDING' on a file whose result block shows completed work) -> byte-identical hash, and NOT flagged as an H1 violation at all -- confirmed this is correct/by-design and not a gap: H1 and --autofix both operate purely on 'is the value one of six legal strings', which INV-6's own spirit and the design's stated scope (section 2.2, 6.1) both limit to; detecting a legal-but-wrong lifecycle state against the file's own result content is a different, harder property this design never claimed to solve, and conflating the two would be scope creep on my part, not a finding. Also tested a genuinely malformed (unparseable) JSON file: File.read/Jason.decode fails inside autofix_file/1's `with`, falls to `_ -> :skip` (line 444) -- the file is neither fixed nor refused at the autofix stage, but the SUBSEQUOUS unconditional lint_file/2 pass (line 299, runs regardless of --autofix) independently catches it as a [PARSE] hard violation, non-zero exit -- confirmed by direct run, hash unchanged. No case produced a silent success or a silent rewrite.

3. --autofix --dir <real corpus> AS A MASS-REWRITE SURFACE -- SECURITY VERDICT: safe as designed, given three independently-verified structural properties, not merely CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR's ergonomics judgement. (a) The rewrite surface is provably narrow: the map is a closed 3-key literal, hardcoded, with FAIL and everything else routed to a refuse branch that never calls write_json!/2 -- there is no pattern-matching or heuristic scoring that could misfire against real content, only exact string equality against three literals. An agent or human running --autofix against handoffs/ cannot make it rewrite anything beyond {PASS,COMPLETE,DONE}->COMPLETED on the top-level status field, confirmed by reading the full function body, not by trusting the design doc's claim. (b) It is not silent: print_autofix_report/1 and print_autofix_refused/1 print every touched (and every refused) file by path and value to stdout on every invocation -- there is no flag to suppress this output, so a mass run leaves an unavoidable log trail in whatever captured the command's stdout (a CI log, a terminal scrollback, an agent's own tool-call transcript in this pipeline's transcript-based audit model). (c) It leaves a git diff: because it's a real file rewrite (not a git-history rewrite), the normal `git diff`/`git status` a reviewer or the next agent would already look at before committing/pushing shows exactly which files changed and exactly what changed in each (a one-line JSON diff: "status": "PASS" -> "status": "COMPLETED") -- this is the answer to 'is per-file reporting enough to make such a run visible': yes, twice over, once in the command's own stdout and independently again in git's own diff, and the two are not redundant since either one alone (a lost terminal scroll, or a `git add -A && git commit` without reading the diff) would still leave the other. What this verdict does NOT cover, named so it isn't silently assumed away: a run's stdout report and git diff visibility both depend on a human or agent actually looking -- neither is a structural (Tier-1/CI-enforced) guarantee against a reviewer skipping the diff, the same Tier-1/2/3 distinction the design itself is careful about for its own two mechanisms. That is a pre-existing property of every git-tracked change in this pipeline (nothing --autofix introduces uniquely) and is bounded by the same CI-green-gate + humanless-pipeline review discipline every other change in this repo already depends on -- not a new gap this feature opens. Restricting --autofix to non-default directories, as the design considered and rejected, would not close that residual gap either (a restricted flag is just as invisible to a reviewer who skips the diff) while reintroducing the 'agent must remember the safe flag' failure this whole issue exists to eliminate -- so I concur with the design's choice on security grounds, not only ergonomics grounds, for this specific reason.

4. CI PATH INTEGRITY -- RE-DERIVED INDEPENDENTLY, CONFIRMED. `git diff main...HEAD -- mix.exs .github/workflows/ci.yml` returned empty output myself (ran it fresh, not copy-pasted from ORCH's claim). Ran bare `mix letflow.lint_handoffs` (no flags) myself: exit 0, final line 'letflow.lint_handoffs: OK -- 0 new violations across 1927 handoff files under "handoffs" (25 pre-existing grandfathered, traced to ISS-0190).' -- 0-new and 25-grandfathered match ORCH's claimed baseline exactly (file count drifted 1923->1927, expected corpus growth from this run's own handoffs, not a defect). Also ran `mix compile --warnings-as-errors` (exit 0) and `mix format --check-formatted` (exit 0) myself.

5. check_registry_coverage/2's dir THREADING -- CONFIRMED NO-OP ON DEFAULT PATH. Read the function body directly (lines 878-904): `dir` is used exactly once, in `Path.relative_to(dir)` when computing disk_run_ids for the H5 report. H5 is report-only and does not participate in the exit code (confirmed by reading run/1's own comment at line 310-314 and the surrounding logic -- hard_new is derived from H1-H4 checks only, never from registry_result). On the default no-flag path dir == @handoffs_dir == "handoffs", identical to the pre-ISS-0440 hardcoded call, and my own no-flag baseline run's H5 output changed only in ways attributable to normal corpus growth (new run_ids from this run's own handoffs), not to any behavioural change from the dir parameter. Confirmed this does not weaken H1-H4 (the actual gate) in any way -- those checks never reference `dir` at all.

Additional confirmations run myself, not inherited: no new dependency (mix.exs/mix.lock diff for this branch is empty; Jason was already a dependency); no network call anywhere in the diff; no shell-out beyond the three pre-existing (unmodified) git-history queries; `git status --porcelain lib/ test/` is clean (my transient probe files lived entirely outside the repo and were deleted after use, never touching lib/ or test/).

Verdict: PASS. All applicable pipeline-integrity properties hold under independent re-derivation, not producer self-report. No BLOCKER found.
